# On the Pleasure of Unfinished Things

There's a particular satisfaction in things left incomplete—not abandoned, but suspended in process. A half-built shelf in the garage. A novel with a bookmark at chapter seven. A song you hum but never finish writing.

We're taught to value completion, the satisfying click of a finished puzzle, the closed loop of a resolved story. But I find myself drawn lately to the middle spaces, the places where potential still outweighs result. An unfinished painting holds every possible version of itself; once complete, it can only be the one thing it became.

This isn't an argument for laziness or perpetual procrastination. It's something else—a recognition that the process often contains more life than the product. The carpenter sanding wood, lost in the rhythm of the work, isn't thinking about the finished table. The writer mid-sentence, chasing a thought before it dissolves, isn't thinking about the published book.

Maybe this is why old sketchbooks feel more alive than gallery walls, why demo tapes sometimes hit harder than polished albums. There's an honesty in the unfinished—you can see the hand that made it, the uncertainty, the searching.

I think about this when I consider my own life: the relationships still being figured out, the skills half-learned, the person I'm still becoming rather than have become. Perhaps wisdom isn't about reaching some finished state of understanding, but about getting comfortable living inside the question, the sketch, the rough draft.

The unfinished thing keeps asking something of you. That's not a flaw. That might be the point.
